Multiscale Contrastive Learning for Node Clustering
Based on Variational Graph Auto-Encoder
Nazila Pourhaji Aghayengejeh , M. A. Balafar , Jafar Tanha , Narjes Nikzad Khasmakhi, and Shervin Minaee
Abstract—Variational graph auto-encoders (VGAEs) are a
key tool for node clustering, but existing models face several
signiﬁcant challenges. These challenges include a mismatch
between inference and generative models after incorporating the
clustering inductive bias, as well as posterior collapse (PC), where
latent representations become overly inﬂuenced by the prior
distribution. In addition, in existing VGAEs, noisy clustering
assignments lead to the feature randomness (FR) challenge,
while the strong tradeoﬀbetween clustering accuracy and recon-
struction quality results in the feature drift (FD) problem. To
address these issues, we propose a multiscale contrastive VGAE
(MCVGAE). This multiscale model combines cluster-level and
graph-level contrastive learning with proximity-level and cluster-
level self-supervised methods. MCVGAE improves the alignment
between the hidden space and the data distribution and prevents
PC. Moreover, it reduces FR and FD more eﬀectively than
existing techniques. Achieving impressive accuracy scores of
79.09% on Cora, 90.04% on ACM, 75.12% on Pubmed, 72.7%
on Citeseer, 74.11% on DBLP, and 59.79% on Wiki clearly
demonstrates the superiority of MCVGAE over 30 state-of-the-
art methods.
Index Terms—Contrastive learning, node clustering, unsuper-
vised learning, variational graph auto-encoder (VGAE).

sections.text: [13] addresses FR by using a vMF prior for structured embeddings, while GMM- VGAE [15] employs a Gaussian mixture model to better capture complex latent distributions. Recent VGAEs failed to present a solution to address FR, FD, PC, and model mismatch. For the first time in 2024, contrastive learning has been integrated with ELBO in CVGAE [6] . CVGAE combines cluster-level and proximity- level self-supervised methods with cluster-level contrastive learning to address the PC, FR, FD, and model mismatch. In CVGAE, a cluster-oriented graph is built during training. This dynamic graph structure allows the clustering results to improve based on the evolving data representation, while the graph structure is modified according to the clustering results. This approach gradually shifts the objective from proximity to cluster-level, improving embeddings and clustering accu- racy, though some limitations remain. The e ff ectiveness of cluster-level contrastive learning strongly depends on cluster- ing accuracy. Clusters with low-accuracy reinforce incorrect relationships in the cluster-oriented graph, leading to subopti- mal representations. Moreover, CVGAE gradually hardens the clustering assignments based on a confidence threshold, which causes the model to focus too much on the current clustering structure and ignore other useful information in the graph. This constraint reduces the model’s flexibility in handling complex graph topologies. Thus, the use of global structural information remains crucial for further improvement. This study proposes multiscale contrastive VGAE (MCV- GAE), a multiscale contrastive learning variational graph auto- encoder that enhances CVGAE by incorporating graph-level contrastive learning. As far as we know, it is the first model to use multiscale contrastive learning in VGAEs. In graph-level contrastive learning, the overall graph embedding—computed as the average of all node embeddings (valid and noisy embeddings)—mitigates the influence of noisy embeddings in cluster-oriented graph, reducing FR. Simultaneously, node embeddings converge toward their own view’s global embed- ding and diverge from the opposite view’s, enhancing the distinction between cluster-oriented and original graphs, which alleviates PC. Aligning node representations with the global summary preserves structural properties relevant for both clustering and reconstruction, addressing FD. This alignment also coordinates encoder outputs with decoder requirements, resolving model mismatch. Thus, MCVGAE reduces the prob- lems of FR, FD, PC, and model mismatch more e ff ectively than CVGAE. The contributions of this article are outlined as follows. 1) This article presents a novel multiscale contrastive learn- ing framework (MCVGAE) that integrates cluster-level and graph-level contrastive learning with cluster-level and proximity-level self-supervised methods in VGAE. This multiscale approach significantly improves the alignment between the hidden latent space and the data distribution, leading to more accurate and robust representations. 2) MCVGAE captures relationships at local and global scales and considers both fine-grained node similar- ities by proximity-level learning and coarse-grained structures via cluster-level and graph-level learnings in representation learning. Therefore, it enhances the expressiveness of the latent space and ensures better generative performance. 3) This multiscale approach handles sparse or noisy graphs more e ff ectively and improves clustering performance in challenging graphs. 4) Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demon- strate MCVGAE’s superior ability to address PC, FD, FR, and model mismatch issues while improving the clustering accuracy over 30 state-of-the-art methods. AGE [27] trains a fully connected neural network to create a clustering- oriented graph. R-DGAE [28] combines two operators in the clustering-reconstruction loss. In DAEGC [29] , an attention- based encoder evaluates the significance of neighboring nodes. In R 2 FGC [30] , a graph di ff usion process captures local con- nectivity beyond direct edges while preserving the relational similarity among nodes within the same clusters. The cluster- level method emphasizes global structure but overlooks local relationships, and it depends heavily on clustering quality; inaccurate cluster assignments degrade the quality of node representations. B. Contrastive Learning Contrastive learning is a self-supervised technique under the framework of pairwise learning [31] . In this approach, the model learns to di ff erentiate between similar (positive) samples and dissimilar (negative) samples [32] . The node-level method generates new graphs using an augmentation technique, increasing similarity between posi- tive samples and decreasing it between negative ones [33] . GraphCL [34] applies four data augmentations to generate a new graph and trains a GNN encoder with a joint projection head using contrastive loss. GRACE [35] generates two graph views and uses the InfoNCE loss [36] to maximize the lower bound of MI between their encoded views. GCA [33] replaces random augmentation with an adaptive method, enhancing GRACE’s performance. BGRL [37] improves scalability by removing negative samples in contrastive learning and trains an online encoder to predict the target encoder’s representa- tions of augmented graph views. MeCoLe [38] generates hard negative samples near the decision boundary, improving the discriminative power of the learned representations. NS4GC [39] aligns nodes with their neighbors in the representation space and employs a semantic-aware sparsification technique to refine the node similarity matrix. Node-level contrastive learning considers distant nodes in the same cluster as neg- atives, losing cluster-level information. Graph augmentations can also degrade embedding quality by distorting structure and content. Graph-level contrastive learning maximizes similarity between node and graph embeddings while minimizing sim- ilarity between the graph and corrupted node embeddings [40] . In MVGRL [41] , a contrastive objective function is employed to maximize MI between node embeddings from one view and graph representations from another. DGI [42] maximizes MI between local and global representations by optimizing a binary cross-entropy loss on both negative and positive samples. MLGCL [43] maximizes MI between the global graph representations of the original graph and the KNN graph constructed from the feature space. LS-GCL [44] model constructs semantic subgraphs for each target node using the personalized pagerank (PPR) algorithm, capturing local structural information beyond just the first-order neighbors. Graph- level contrastive learning focuses on global structure, limiting its ability to capture local relationships crucial for cluster boundaries. Some studies have utilized cluster-level contrastive learn- ing. CLAGC [46] generates a KNN graph and utilizes edge betweenness centrality to construct contrastive views while preserving cluster structures. In SCGC [47] , an influence augmented contrastive (IAC) loss leverages a novel distance metric called “influence,” which aggregates multihop neigh- borhood information to capture both local and global structural dependencies. S3-CL [48] employs the structural contrastive learning with multiscale feature propagation for augmentation and uses Bayesian semantic contrastive learning to improve intracluster compactness and intercluster separability. CVGAE [6] progressively constructs a cluster-oriented graph where edges are added or removed based on reliable clustering assignments. It then contrasts the learned representations from this graph with those from the original graph. Although CVGAE enhances the clustering accuracy, it has key limitations. It depends on clustering assignments, which are often inaccurate during the early epochs of training. These unreliable assignments reinforce incorrect relationships in a cluster-oriented graph and degrade the quality of the Authorized licensed use limited to: University of Lancashire. Furthermore, the progressive hardening of cluster assignments based on a confidence threshold can lead to over-reliance on the current clustering structure, potentially overlooking valuable topological or feature-based signals out- side the confident subset. This issue limits its ability to adapt to a complex graph. To address these limitations, this article proposes MCVGAE, which integrates graph-level contrastive learning into CVGAE. In graph-level contrastive learning, computing the overall graph embedding by averaging all node embeddings helps to suppress the e ff ect of noisy nodes in cluster-oriented graphs, reducing FR. In addition, node embed- dings are aligned with their view’s global representation and pushed away from the opposite view’s, sharpening the contrast between cluster-oriented and original graphs and mitigating PC. This alignment maintains key structural features needed for both clustering and reconstruction, addressing FD. It also synchronizes encoder outputs with decoder needs, e ff ectively resolving model mismatch. Table I illustrates the comparison of contrastive learning-based models. C. Variational Graph Auto-Encoders VGAE is an unsupervised learning framework for graph data based on the variational auto-encoder (VAE) [49] . Some VGAEs focus on improving the encoder. N-VGAE [20] models latent variables with a Gaussian posterior. In SIG- VGAE [9] , semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) creates a hierarchical structure where the posterior parameters are drawn from a non-Gaussian implicit distribution. S-VGAE [13] adopts a von Mises–Fisher prior for better clustering on hyperspheres. VGAE-AMI [10] integrates an adversarial MI learning framework into the encoding process. IVGAE [11] , enhances VGAE by incorporating multiorder GCNs (MoGCN) in the encoder. Some other VGAEs emphasize enhancing the decoder. In GRAPHITE [50] , an iterative graph refinement strategy modi- fies the decoder. This strategy generates an intermediate graph using the inner product, which is gradually refined through message passing in a GNN. In GDN-VAE [51] , the decoder is constructed using a graph deconvolution operation. In this model, spectral deconvolution is applied with an inverse filter to recover high-frequency signals.

The adjacency matrix A = { a ij } ∈{ 0 , 1 } N × N shows the topology structure of the graph, where a i j = 1 if ( ν i , ν j ) ∈ E . The degree matrix D = diag( d 1 , d 2 , . . . , d N ) ∈ R N × N shows the degree of every node. The symmetric nor- malized adjacency matrix is ˜ A ∈ R N × N and is calculated by ˜ A = D − (1 / 2) ( A + I ) D − (1 / 2) , where I ∈ R N × N denotes an identity matrix. The nodes of G can be divided into K clusters. The vector Cl ∈{ 1 , . . . , K } N indicates the cluster assignment for di ff erent nodes, where cl i denotes the cluster of the i th node. B. Overview of MCVGAE Similar to CVGAE [6] , MCVGAE consists of pretraining and training. During pretraining, the model is optimized using an ELBO combining reconstruction and regularization terms. In the training phase, a three-part variational lower bound—consisting of the ELBO term, a clustering objective, and a contrastive learning term—is used to train the model. To better capture global structure, we extend CVGAE [6] by adding graph-level contrastive learning. This new mul- tiscale approach combines cluster-level and proximity-level self-supervised methods with graph-level and cluster-level contrastive learning to address the issues of PC, FR, FD, and model mismatch. The overall framework of MCVGAE is illustrated in Fig. 1 . Each part is explained in detail below. C. Encoder–Decoder Architecture in MCVGAE The MCVGAE comprises an encoder (EN) and a decoder (DE). The encoder is a GCN that maps graph features and topology into a low-dimensional matrix Z ∈ R N × d [52] . IV. E XPERIMENTS A. Datasets Unlike supervised learning, which splits data into training, validation, and testing sets, clustering focuses on uncovering hidden patterns rather than generalizing to unseen data [6] . Following CVGAE [6] , MCVGAE is designed to cluster the training data directly, and all data in this study are used for training without separate validation or testing sets. MCVGAE is evaluated on six widely used datasets: Cora [53] , PubMed [53] , Citeseer [53] , ACM [25]

sections.text: [25] , and Wiki [54] . Cora, Citeseer, and PubMed [20] are citation networks in which nodes represent papers and edges indicate citation links. Wiki [55] is a webpage network, where nodes represent web pages connected by links. In Cora and Citeseer, the features are binary word vectors, while PubMed and Wiki are described using tfidf-weighted word vectors. The ACM dataset consists of scholarly papers from the ACM digital library, where an edge connects two papers if they have a common author. The DBLP dataset, sourced from the DBLP computer science bibliography, is a network of authors connected by edges when they share a co-author. Authors’ features are represented as bag-of-words vectors derived from keywords, and they are categorized into database, data mining, machine learning, and information retrieval [56] . A description of these datasets is shown in Table II . For each dataset, we compute the density of graph A based on the following formula: Density = 2 × E N ( N − 1) × 100 . (28) B. Evaluation Metric Accuracy (ACC), normalized MI (NMI), adjusted rand index (ARI), macro-averaged F1 score (F1), purity (Pur), and precision (Pre) are the metrics utilized to evaluate the quality of the MCVGAE model. The results are reported as percentages, with higher values indicating better model quality. In addition, the Λ FR , Λ FD , and AU criteria are defined to assess the levels of FD, FR, and the number of hidden units. Λ FR is determined by the cosine of the angle between the gradient of the pseudo-supervised loss, derived from pseudo- labels, and the gradient of the supervised loss, calculated using the true labels. This metric is expressed as follows: Λ FR = cos � ∂ L clus ( P ) ∂ W , ∂ L clus ( Q ) ∂ W � (29) where L clus denotes the clustering loss, P represents the clustering assignment matrix, and Q denotes the matrix of the true clustering assignments. The values of Λ FR are within the range [0, 1]. Λ FD is the cosine of the angle between the gradient of the general-purpose self-supervised loss and the task-specific self-supervised loss. This metric quantifies the degree of competition between these two losses, providing insight into their deviation from the clustering objective. In this study, Λ FD is used to analyze the competition between the gradients of two cross-entropy losses: the vanilla reconstruction of the original graph A , represented by L vr ( A ), and the construction of the clustering-oriented graph A gen , represented as L vr ( A gen ). The level of FD is captured by the following metric: Λ FD = cos � ∂ L vr ( A ) ∂ W , ∂ L vr ( A gen ) ∂ W � . (30) The intuitive explanation of Λ FR and Λ FD is illustrated in Fig. 4 . The PC problem arises when most hidden units fail to extract useful information from the input signal, which is caused by the regularization term in the ELBO. The VGAE extensions discussed fall into three categories: 1) models enhancing encoding (e.g., N-VGAE, S-VGAE, GMM-VGAE, D-VGAE, and SI-VGAE); 2) models improv- ing decoding (e.g., graphite and GDN-VAE); and 3) models improving both encoding and decoding (e.g., CVGAE). CVGAE boosts encoding via contrastive learning and refines decoding by reconstructing a cluster-oriented graph. Similar to CVGAE, MCVGAE improves both encoder and decoder performance. MCVGAE leverages graph-level con- trastive learning to amplify the distinction between positive and negative views, mitigating the influence of noisy clus- tering predictions. As a result, it alleviates FR and PC more e ff ectively than CVGAE. In addition, graph-level contrastive learning maximizes MI between node embeddings and a global graph summary, enabling the representations to capture the overall graph structure rather than just local proximities. This encourages the encoder to preserve global structural properties relevant to both clustering and reconstruction. Consequently, MCVGAE reduces model mismatch and FD caused by an overemphasis on local or proximity-level information. There- fore, MCVGAE has the best performance among the models in Tables IV and V across all datasets. The Cora dataset is a well-structured citation network with relatively clear cluster boundaries. As a result, the perfor- mance gap between MCVGAE and CVGAE is smaller (0.5% improvement). In such datasets, the local graph structure and node features already provide su ffi cient information for clustering, and the additional global refinements introduced by MCVGAE have a more limited impact. MCVGAE achieves a 0.96% improvement in accuracy over CVGAE on PubMed. This improvement can be attributed to MCVGAE’s ability to leverage both local and global structural information e ff ectively. While PubMed’s clearer cluster boundaries reduce the impact of noise and sparsity compared to other datasets, the integration of cluster- level contrastive learning allows MCVGAE to refine local node embeddings by emphasizing intra-cluster similarities. Simultaneously, graph-level contrastive learning aligns the overall graph structure with node embeddings, enhancing the global representation for more discriminative clustering. The models in Table VI are categorized based on the level of abstraction they use for self-supervision: Proximity- level, graph-level, node-level, integration of graph-level and cluster-level, integration of proximity-level and cluster-level, integration of node-level and cluster-level. Proximity-level methods rely on local structure, ignoring global context and are prone to FD due to conflicts with the clustering objective. Node-level methods are prone to FR because they treat all nodes except the target node as negatives, which can lead to noisy gradients. Cluster-level methods are prone to FR due to their reliance on pseudo-labels generated by clus- tering algorithms. Graph-level methods often overlook fine- grained structural information, which is crucial for e ff ective clustering. MCVGAE integrates proximity-level and cluster-level self- supervised methods with cluster-level and graph-level con- trastive learning and balances them, reducing the risk of FD. MCVGAE includes mechanisms to mitigate FR by gradually refining clustering assignments and focus- ing on reliable nodes. It also addresses PC and model mismatch by introducing a contrastive term that pre- vents the latent representations from collapsing to a prior distribution. 3) Robustness: In this section, we explore the performance of MCVGAE by adding Gaussian noise with noise level of 0.6. Specifically, we add Gaussian noise to the features of a certain percentage of graph nodes (5%, 10%, 15%, and 20%) that are randomly selected. The performance of CVGAE and MCVGAE after adding noise are shown in Fig. 5 . According to Fig. 5 , MCVGAE exhibits a reason- able level of robustness to noise on the CiteSeer dataset, retaining a significant portion of its accuracy even under substantial noise conditions. In contrast, on the Wiki dataset, MCVGAE’s performance dropped more sharply, indicating greater sensitivity to noise. The Wiki dataset has a higher density, more classes, and a larger feature dimension compared with Citeseer that introduces challenges such as complexity, more noise, and overlapping clusters compared with Cite- seer. Adding noise to the Wiki dataset further exacerbates these issues, leading to a greater performance decline. While MCVGAE outperforms CVGAE under noise, results highlight the need for improved adaptability to challenging real-world datasets. 4) Dynamic Learning Process: We analyze MCVGAE’s dynamic learning on Citeseer and Wiki, comparing its per- Authorized licensed use limited to: University of Lancashire. This indicates the clustering term is more e ff ective on Wiki, because many connections in Wiki exist between nodes from di ff erent clusters, and the clustering loss helps to restructure this pattern. In Fig. 9(c) and (g) , Λ FR is higher for MCVGAE- Cluster than MCVGAE during the first 150 epochs on Citeseer and Wiki. This di ff erence is attributed to MCVGAE-Cluster having more high-confidence nodes and fewer low-confidence nodes than MCVGAE during the initial epochs. Also, MCV- GAE and MCVGAE-Graph show similar trends, highlighting the stronger impact of graph-level over cluster-level contrastive learning in reducing FR. In graph-level contrastive learning, averaging all node embeddings (valid and noisy) reduces the impact of invalid ones. Minimizing the gap between cluster- oriented and overall graph embeddings mitigates clustering noise and reduces FR. 2) Feature Drift: Λ FD measures the FD level, where higher values indicate lower FD and better model performance. In Fig. 9(b) , MCVGAE-FR performs best during the first 60 epochs on Citeseer, while MCVGAE excels afterward. On Citeseer, MCVGAE-FD, and MCVGAE-FR show similar performance, which is attributed to the alignment of the recon- struction and clustering losses on this dataset. In Fig. 9(f) , on Wiki, MCVGAE-FR shows the worst performance due to the lack of a mechanism to address FD, as the clustering term cannot compensate for the loss of proximity-level infor- mation. MCVGAE’s results also confirm the e ff ectiveness of graph-level contrastive learning in mitigating FD. In Fig. 9(d) and (h) , the Λ FD value for MCVGAE exceeds that of MCVGAE-Cluster and MCVGAE-Graph on both Wiki and Citeseer. Moreover, MCVGAE and MCVGAE-Graph dis- play comparable trends, underscoring the greater influence of graph-level contrastive learning compared to cluster-level. Graph-level contrastive learning aligns node representations with a global summary. This helps preventing FD caused by over-reliance on local or proximity-based information. 3) Posterior Collapse: Fig. 10 shows the AU di ff erences on Citeseer and Wiki. In Fig. 10(a) , for Citeseer, except during the initial 60 epochs, the di ff erence between MCVGAE and MCVGAE-Cluster (CVGAE) is positive and shows an upward trend, indicating that the AU value for MCVGAE is higher than for CVGAE. This shows that the number of inactive units during MCVGAE training is reduced compared with CVGAE. A similar trend is observed for Wiki in Fig. 10(c) . Moreover, an upward trend is also observed in the comparison between MCVGAE and MCVGAE-Graph in Fig. 10(b) for Citeseer and Fig. 10(d) for Wiki, indicating that integrating cluster-level with graph-level contrastive learning significantly reduces the number of inactive units during training. In MCVGAE, graph- level contrastive learning maximizes MI between node and graph embeddings, enhancing the distinction between cluster- oriented and original graphs and thereby alleviating PC. 4) Sensitivity Analysis: To evaluate the sensitivity to key hyperparameters, we report MCVGAE’s accuracy and NMI on the Wiki and Citeseer datasets. Specifically, we test M = [1 , 10 , 20 , 30] and α = [0 . 15 , 0 . 2 , 0 . 25 , 0 . 3] across all datasets. As shown in Fig. 11 , despite significant variations in these hyperparameters, the accuracy of MCVGAE fluc- tuates between 1% and 5% on the Citeseer dataset, and between 0.33% and 4% on the Wiki dataset. While these fluctuations may appear notable, they are consistent with the inherent variability observed in CVGAE [6] , which shows accuracy changes of up to 6% on Citeseer. In sparse graphs like Citeseer (density = 0.08%), small changes in clustering assignments can significantly alter the graph topology, ampli- fying sensitivity to hyperparameters such as the confidence threshold α and update interval M .
